title: Acquired cytomegalovirus in children: pathogen, bystander, or immune trainer?
abstract: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is one of the most common infections worldwide, with acquisition occurring predominantly in early childhood (younger than 5 years). Although congenital CMV is a recognised cause of neurodevelopmental impairment, the consequences of postnatally acquired CMV in children remain poorly defined and are often assumed to be benign. However, accumulating evidence suggests that acquired CMV infection is biologically active even when clinically silent, with the capacity to shape immune ontogeny, influence immune responses to other pathogens and vaccines, and alter health trajectories across the life course. In this Review, we examine the epidemiology, transmission pathways, immune responses, and clinical consequences of acquired CMV infection in childhood. We synthesise evidence to evaluate whether acquired CMV acts as a driver of pathology, a neutral bystander, or a beneficial immune trainer. The effects of CMV are highly context-dependent, determined by the timing of acquisition, host immune maturity, maternal health, co-infections, and broader social and environmental factors. Evidence of harm is strongest in infants with heightened biological or contextual risk, such as infants born preterm and those living with or exposed to HIV, whereas effects in children who are immunocompetent are heterogeneous and often clinically silent. Acquired CMV should be understood as a context-dependent immune modifier rather than a uniformly benign or pathogenic infection. This reframing of acquired CMV has important implications for policy and research. Universal intervention is unlikely to be appropriate; instead, targeted CMV prevention and treatment strategies for populations at high risk of CMV infection and severe disease integrated into maternal and child health programmes could offer the greatest benefit. Defining high-risk populations and critical windows for intervention should be prioritised to translate emerging evidence into improvements in childhood morbidity and equity.

title: Parent Comfort With Artificial Intelligence-Led Behavioral Therapy for Their Child
abstract:
This survey study assesses the comfort of parents with pediatric behavioral therapy led by artificial intelligence (AI) by evaluating results from a cross-sectional survey of US adults with at least 1 child aged 5 to 17 years.

Shortages in pediatric behavioral health services have increased interest in leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) for support, and platforms that offer to deliver these services are increasingly accessible to children and adolescents. In a 2025 national survey, 19.2% of US youth aged 12 to 21 years reported using AI chatbots for mental health advice, often without disclosure to parents or clinicians. Pediatric behavioral therapy requires clinical evaluation, family involvement, safety planning, and clear escalation procedures. The American Psychological Association has cautioned that adolescent AI use raises concerns about developmental vulnerability, inaccurate health information, and privacy. Parents’ views may inform how AI-led behavioral therapy is governed for children, yet parent comfort with this approach is unknown. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of US adults in November 2025 through the OutbreaksNearMe participatory surveillance platform using a nonprobability end-page river sample on SurveyMonkey, with survey weights approximating US Census demographic targets for age, gender, race and ethnicity, education, and income. The analytic sample included adults with at least 1 child aged 5 to 17 years. The Boston Children’s Hospital institutional review board approved the study, which followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline. Participants provided electronic informed consent. Participants self-selected race and ethnicity from survey categories for weighting and adjustment. The primary outcome was an ordered 4-level response to “How comfortable would you be with a therapy session led by an AI for your children?” Options were “not comfortable at all,” “not too comfortable,” “somewhat comfortable,” and “very comfortable.” Parallel items asked about therapy and primary care for themselves. Associations with higher comfort were estimated using survey-weighted cumulative-logit ordinal logistic regression among parents with complete data. Models adjusted for parent age, gender, race and ethnicity, educational attainment, household income, chronic illness, health care satisfaction, household child age groups, and the AI-related measures reported in the Figure and Table . The proportional-odds assumption was assessed qualitatively using threshold-specific estimates and graphical summaries. Weighted proportions and 95% CIs used logit-transformed Taylor-linearized standard errors. Analyses used R version 4.6.0 (R Foundation). Results Among 3102 respondents, 584 had at least 1 child aged 5 to 17 years, and 572 responded to the primary outcome regarding comfort level with AI-led behavioral therapy for their child. After weighting, the sample was 53.3% female, 45.7% male, and 1.0% not listed or nonconforming; 6.2% were Asian or Pacific Islander, 12.0% Black, 23.6% Hispanic, 54.2% White, and 3.9% other. Weighted comfort levels were 47.2% not comfortable at all (95% CI, 42.1%-52.3%), 28.8% not too comfortable (95% CI, 24.5%-33.6%), 16.2% somewhat comfortable (95% CI, 12.7%-20.5%), and 7.8% very comfortable (95% CI, 5.3%-11.3%). In the multivariable ordinal regression model (n = 554), higher comfort was associated with parents’ own comfort with AI-led behavioral therapy for themselves (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 20.94; 95% CI, 9.78-44.86) and AI-led primary care for themselves (aOR, 3.78; 95% CI, 2.16-6.59). Higher comfort was also associated with expectations that AI would perform better than (aOR, 10.12; 95% CI, 4.38-23.38) or about the same as (aOR, 3.31; 95% CI, 1.95-5.61) medical professionals for pediatric behavioral therapy. Child receipt of behavioral therapy in the past year was also associated with higher comfort (aOR, 2.07; 95% CI, 1.22-3.50). General AI use by parents and children was not associated with comfort. When asked which factors would matter most in deciding about AI-led behavioral therapy for their child, parents (n = 546) most frequently selected accuracy of diagnosis (58.5%), level of empathy (49.4%), recommendation from a medical professional (46.8%), and confidentiality and privacy (43.7%); cost (32.8%), scheduling flexibility (29.5%), and appointment wait time (27.7%) were selected less often. Discussion In this cross-sectional survey of US parents, approximately three-quarters were not comfortable at all or not too comfortable with AI-led behavioral therapy for their child. Higher comfort was most strongly associated with parents’ own comfort with AI-led health care and expectations that AI would perform similarly to or better than medical professionals, with prior child behavioral therapy also associated. These findings add the parent perspective to prior work on youth AI chatbot use. Parent acceptance may depend more on AI-related health care trust than on convenience or familiarity alone; general AI use was unrelated to comfort. Diagnostic accuracy, empathy, professional recommendation, and privacy were selected as priorities more often than cost, scheduling flexibility, or wait time. Clinician recommendations may be a modifiable lever for acceptance yet remain uncharacterized for pediatric AI-led therapy. Limitations Limitations include the nonprobability sample, modest sample size limiting precision and assessment of subgroup heterogeneity, and unmeasured familiarity with health care AI. Comfort may not reflect actual use, appropriateness, or safety. Cross-sectional data preclude causal inference, and parent comfort for self and child may reflect the same underlying construct. Conclusions This study found that most parents reported low comfort with AI-led behavioral therapy for their children. As these tools scale, policy should emphasize rigorous clinical evaluation, privacy protections, clinician and family oversight, and escalation pathways to earn parental trust.

title: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA Vaccination in Pregnancy and Child Neurodevelopment at 18 to 30 Months
abstract:
This study evaluates whether there is an association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopmental measures.

Key Points Question Is maternal SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA vaccination during pregnancy associated with offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18 to 30 months of age? Findings In this cohort study of 217 matched pairs, median Ages and Stages Questionnaire, Third Edition (ASQ-3) total scores were similar between children of vaccinated and unvaccinated participants. No significant differences were observed in secondary neurodevelopmental measures. Meaning These findings support continued recommendations for SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA vaccination during pregnancy.

Importance Little is known about neurodevelopmental outcomes of children exposed to SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine during pregnancy. Evidence on long-term offspring outcomes after in utero exposure to SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination is needed to inform vaccine recommendations in pregnancy. Objective To evaluate whether there is an association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopmental measures. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, prospective, cohort study of 18- to 30-month-old children was conducted at 14 centers of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network from 2024 through 2025. Women who received a SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine during or within 30 days prior to pregnancy (exposed) were matched with women who did not (unexposed) by delivery site, delivery date, insurance status, and race and ethnicity. These data were analyzed from June 2025 to May 2026. Exposures Maternal receipt of at least 1 dose of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine during, or within 30 days prior to, the index pregnancy vs no SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during pregnancy or within 30 days prior. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was Ages and Stages Questionnaire version 3 (ASQ-3) total score, which was deemed to be equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups if the 90% CI of the median difference was between −10 and 10. Secondary outcomes included domain-specific ASQ-3 scores, the Child Behavior Checklist, Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, and Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire scores. Results Of 3956 screened, 271 exposed and 240 unexposed children were enrolled. Matching on all characteristics was possible in 217 pairs. Of the 434 children enrolled, 258 (59.4%) were Non-Hispanic White, 96 (22.1%) Non-Hispanic Black, 52 (12.0%) Hispanic, and 28 (6.5%) were not represented by any of the above racial or ethnic groups. Median age at assessment was 25.8 [24.6 to 28.3] months, 221 were female (50.9%), and 213 were male (49.1%). Exposed mothers were more likely to be nulliparous; their children were slightly younger at assessment and more likely to have been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2. The primary outcome of ASQ-3 score was equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups (255 vs 260, adjusted median difference, −3.4; 90% CI, −9.8 to 3.0). There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance In this multicenter cohort study, ASQ-3 scores were equivalent between 18- to 30-month-old children whose mothers did or did not receive mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or immediately prior to pregnancy. These findings support continued recommendations for SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy.

title: Mobile Units for Integrated Addiction and HIV Prevention Services for People Who Inject Drugs: The HPTN 094 Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
Key Points Question Does providing 26 weeks of integrated HIV prevention and addiction services for people who inject drugs using peer navigation delivered in a mobile unit produce superior outcomes compared to peer navigation to existing standard-of-care community-based services alone? Findings In this randomized clinical trial, HIV prevention and addiction outcomes were similar between study arms, though the intervention showed a greater reduction in all-cause mortality compared with standard of care. Meaning The findings suggest that integrated mobile service delivery models may reduce all-cause mortality for people who inject drugs.

This randomized clinical trial evaluates the use of preexposure prophylaxis for HIV and medications for opioid use disorder among individuals who inject drugs.

Importance Integrated models to deliver HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) for people who inject drugs are needed. Objective To determine whether integrated PrEP and MOUD services delivered on a mobile unit with manualized peer navigation improved PrEP and MOUD use compared with peer navigation to existing community-based services. Design, Setting, and Participants This 2-group, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted between May 2021 and September 2024 in Houston, Texas; Los Angeles, California; New York, New York; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; and Washington, DC, among people aged 18 years and older currently injecting drugs, without HIV, with OUD, and not taking MOUD but willing to consider MOUD. Interventions The intervention arm (n = 203) consisted of 26 weeks of manualized peer navigation plus integrated PrEP, MOUD, and limited clinical and supportive services delivered on a mobile unit. The active control arm (n = 206) consisted of 26 weeks of manualized peer navigation to available community-based PrEP, MOUD, harm reduction, and supportive services. Main Outcomes and Measures The co–primary outcomes were PrEP use and MOUD use at 26 weeks. Secondary outcomes included PrEP and MOUD use at 52 weeks, HIV incidence, and all-cause mortality. Results Of 842 people who inject drugs who were screened, 409 were randomized: 134 (32.8%) female; 146 (11.2%) aged 30 years and younger vs older than 30 years. At the 26-week visit, the intervention and active control arms were similar for confirmed PrEP use: 11/203 (5.4%) vs 6/206 (2.9%) and MOUD use: 30/203 (14.8%) vs 22/206 (10.7%), respectively. At the 52-week visit, intervention and active control arms were similar for confirmed PrEP and MOUD: 4/203 (2.0%) vs 4/206 (1.9%) and MOUD use: 27/203 (13.3%) vs 29/206 (14.1%). One HIV acquisition occurred in the intervention and 2 in the active control arms; HIV incidence rate of 0.9 per 100 person-years (95% CI, 0.2-2.6). Four deaths were confirmed in the intervention arm and 13 in the active control arm (hazard ratio, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.1-0.9; P = .03). Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, mobile delivery of integrated HIV prevention, addiction, and navigation services did not improve primary outcomes beyond peer navigation alone. The significantly lower all-cause death rate at 52 weeks in the intervention arm bears replication for delivering integrated PrEP and MOUD services to people who inject drugs. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04804072

Introduction Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a major driver of HIV acquisition in the US and a leading contributor to mortality among people who use opioids, whether alone or in combination with stimulants. Beyond HIV acquisition and overdose, people who inject drugs experience elevated risks of comorbid conditions, including hepatitis C, bacterial infections related to nonsterile injection practices, injection-related wounds, and other sexually transmitted infections. People who inject drugs face substantial barriers to accessing key services and support necessary for consistent engagement in HIV prevention and addiction treatment. These barriers include poverty, unstable housing, food insecurity, and limited access to health care, all of which impede regular use of HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for OUD (MOUD). Siloed medical and addiction treatment systems further restrict access by fragmenting care for primary health services, HIV PrEP, and MOUD. Mobile units offer a way to address multiple barriers faced by people who inject drugs in accessing integrated services, including HIV prevention, MOUD, primary care, and social services. Mobile unit-based care differs from care based in conventional brick-and-mortar settings for people who inject drugs along key features of location, integration, immediacy, and service proximity. Yet, rigorous evaluation of mobile unit-based interventions for people who inject drugs remains limited. This study tests whether advantages of integrated HIV and MOUD services using a mobile unit combined with peer navigation would produce statistically significant improvements in primary outcomes of PrEP and MOUD compared to peer navigation to existing standard of care, community-based services alone for people who inject drugs in 5 US cities. Methods Trial Design and Oversight HPTN 094 was a 2-arm, individually randomized, controlled, open-label study that evaluated whether an integrated intervention delivered in a mobile unit improved use of HIV PrEP and MOUD at 26 and 52 weeks ( Figure 1 ). The trial protocol and statistical analysis plan are in Supplement 1 . A single institutional review board, Advarra, provided oversight of the research. Biannual data monitoring oversight was provided by an independent study monitoring committee at the HPTN. All participants provided written informed consent. The study followed the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials ( CONSORT ) reporting guideline. Participants Eligibility criteria included current injection drug use, being aged 18 years and older, the ability to provide informed consent, not currently using but willing to use MOUD, self-reported sharing injection equipment, or having condomless sex in the last 3 months with people with HIV or persons of unknown HIV serostatus, and being able and willing to provide adequate contact information of a person or persons who could help locate participants for follow-up visits. Participants were excluded from the study if they self-reported MOUD in the past 30 days as part of a treatment program or if they were enrolled in another interventional study. Although people with HIV were recruited and randomized, enrollment numbers were insufficient to support rigorous analysis in that group. Study Sites HPTN 094 was conducted in Houston, Texas; Los Angeles, California; New York, New York; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; and Washington, DC. The cities represented diverse large urban contexts with substantial HIV and overdose risks among people who inject drugs. Study sites were selected based on prior experience conducting research on HIV prevention and addiction for people who inject drugs, on geographic diversity, and on HIV prevalence in people who inject drugs. Mobile Units Los Angeles, Houston, and New York chose identical 33-ft medical units that contained an examination table, space for processing laboratory samples, and a toilet; Philadelphia and Washington, DC, chose 26-ft, similarly equipped medical units. Data collection during screening, enrollment, week 26, and week 52 occurred in the mobile unit for all participants. Mobile Unit Placement Preimplementation activities prior to study start-up were conducted by the research team in each city to develop data-driven, community-focused maps using HIV and overdose data, and the location of available community health care services to identify geographic locations where people who inject drugs might best access the mobile units. Locations were intended to facilitate access for actively injecting people who use drugs who lacked a source of care. Recruitment Participants were recruited through street-based outreach at mobile unit locations, community-based recruitment events, incentivized peer referral, and social media. Purposive methods were used to compile a sample with preset target percentages of 25% women and 25% younger (<30 years) participants. Total compensation for completing all research visits was $175 in Houston; $200 in New York, $210 in Philadelphia, $350 in Los Angeles, and $360 in Washington, DC. Screening Screening involved assessments to determine eligibility, including confirmation of OUD diagnosis (clinical interview and DSM-5 checklist), active drug injection activity (recent injection marks), HIV status (rapid antibody point-of-care tests and laboratory-based confirmation), and recent opioid use (urine point-of-care test for opioids; laboratory-based test for fentanyl). Intervention Arm Participants assigned to the intervention arm received 26 weeks of integrated HIV, addiction, and supportive services with peer navigation facilitation of these services, all delivered in a mobile unit (eTable 1 in Supplement 2 ). Peer navigation sessions linked participants to available community services if desired. Medical services delivered on the unit were (1) access to oral PrEP for people without HIV with persons assigned female sex at birth receiving emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate; persons assigned male sex at birth receiving emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (eAppendix 1 in Supplement 2 ). Long-acting cabotegravir for PrEP was not provided by the study; long-acting cabotegravir use was assessed at each study visit and (2) immediate access to MOUD (sublingual buprenorphine provided on-unit or by prescription; facilitated referral to methadone clinic). In addition to facilitated access to MOUD, people who inject drugs with polysubstance use involving stimulants (methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine) were referred to local stimulant treatment and 12-step programs. Active Control Arm Because a uniform standard for delivering integrated PrEP and MOUD to people who inject drugs who are out of treatment is not consistently available, the active control arm received 26 weeks of manualized peer navigation to facilitate linking participants to available services at brick-and-mortar agencies. The scope of services identified and referred in the active control arm paralleled services provided to the intervention arm in the mobile unit. The active control arm provided an ethically acceptable and clinically beneficial comparison condition to no navigation or to no referrals Peer navigation services were delivered virtually or in community spaces away from the mobile unit, such as in parks or near food banks and fast food restaurants. Peer Navigation Peer navigators were hired locally and had personal lived experience of OUD, including injection drug use, or had shared community background involving addiction and recovery with people who inject drugs. The published peer navigation model was informed by systems, self-determination, empowerment, shared decision-making, and social support theories of behavior change (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 2 ). A reference manual for supervisors based on the model-guided navigation sessions aided implementation across sites. Fidelity-supporting procedures for using the navigation model included peer navigators completing 2 weeks of online and in-person training on the model and the study prior to delivering services. Peer navigators provided services to participants in both arms and were supervised by a senior staff member at each site. Peer navigation supervisors from each site met monthly with an expert with extensive experience in training and supervising peer navigators to monitor adherence to the peer navigation model and to support navigators in monitoring their own recovery journeys. Peer navigators met with participants, established rapport, conducted needs assessments, and made referrals to and assisted in accessing services. All participants completed 5 required sessions: (1) MOUD and harm reduction; (2) HIV PrEP; (3) barriers and facilitators to integrated health care; (4) housing, food security, hygiene; and (5) sexual risk behaviors. Additional sessions included these topics: (1) injection risk reduction/drug splitting; (2) stimulants and other substances; (3) alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other downers; and (4) depression and stigma. Dose of peer navigation was measured by number of sessions completed (required and elective), session length (in minutes), and session topics. After 26 weeks, no peer navigation services were provided for either arm. Study Assessments Self-reported demographic characteristics (age, sex assigned at birth, race, ethnicity) and behavioral variables (housing status, access to health care, mental health, criminal justice engagement, drug and alcohol use, overdose experiences, drug treatment experience, and personal connections and support) were captured on case report forms at enrollment, week 26, and week 52. Sensitive information was collected via computer-assisted self-interview, including sexual behavior, medication adherence, stigma, violence, and sexual abuse. Reported deaths were verified by death certificate or medical examiner report, when feasible. Laboratory Methods Biomarkers of recent drug use at screening and follow-ups were measured via antibody-based urine dipsticks that assessed organic and synthetic opioids, oxycodone, cocaine, methamphetamine, amphetamine, and benzodiazepines. Urine screens for fentanyl were conducted via local laboratories. Blood specimens were collected at weeks 0, 26, and 52 and tested in local laboratories. Plasma, urine, and dried blood spots were collected at study visits for HIV confirmatory testing, PrEP, and detection of illicit or nonprescribed drugs. A biomarker confirmed methadone testing was determined using HPTN Laboratory Center–derived urine measurements. Plasma samples were used to assess adherence to buprenorphine. Testing was performed at the HPTN Laboratory Center (Johns Hopkins University) and described in detail in eAppendix 1 in Supplement 2 . Statistical Analysis The study had 2 co–primary outcomes. The primary HIV prevention outcome was the proportion of enrolled participants who returned for the week 26 visit and had biomarker-verified evidence of PrEP use. The primary drug use outcome was the proportion of enrolled participants who attended the week 26 visit and had biomarker-verified evidence of MOUD use (buprenorphine or methadone) and a current prescription for buprenorphine or proof of attendance at a methadone clinic. Secondary outcomes included PrEP and MOUD use at 52-week visits, HIV incidence, overdose-related mortality, and all-cause mortality. Sample sizes were calculated to provide 90% power to detect 15-point differences in PrEP and MOUD use at 26-week visits, with 5% type I error.
